The central question is whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can faithfully decompose neural network activations when the underlying representation is superimposed—that is, when multiple features are simultaneously active and their linear combinations occupy overlapping directions in activation space. The expert also worries about density-dependent phase transitions: at low co-activation rates the SAE behaves well, but past some empirical threshold (which varies with dictionary size and L1 coefficient), suppression cascades non-linearly, meaning evaluations run at moderate density give false confidence that collapses at deployment-scale activation regimes.

When you ablate or steer a bisecting SAE latent, the downstream causal signature is characteristically bifurcated: you simultaneously perturb two distinct computational circuits, producing effect profiles across downstream components (attention heads, MLP outputs, logit differences) that are a superposition of two separable causal graphs—concretely, you'd see activation patching restore partial behavior on two different minimal circuit subsets rather than one clean circuit, and the explained variance from the intervention decomposes into two interpretable chunks that don't co-vary. Wang et al.'s path patching framework (2022, IOI circuit) provides the operational machinery here, but the key addition required is feature-context stratification at patch time, which standard path patching protocols omit because they aggregate over input distributions that mix both feature contexts. The repulsion penalty is genuinely blind to the distinction between artifactual similarity (two atoms collapsed onto a bisecting direction) and intrinsic feature similarity (two genuinely distinct but semantically near-duplicate features the model represents in nearly identical directions, such as "Barack Obama" and "Obama" as separate token-level features in a large LM)—and in the latter case, repulsion actively distorts the dictionary by forcing atoms into directions that reduce reconstruction fidelity for one of the near-duplicate features, effectively re-introducing suppression through geometric displacement rather than L1 pressure. The empirical signature of this distortion is detectable via causal intervention asymmetry post-repulsion: if two atoms were genuinely near-duplicate features forced apart by repulsion, ablating either atom should produce similar downstream causal effects (because they reference the same circuit), whereas if repulsion successfully resolved a collapse, ablating the two new atoms should produce dissimilar causal footprints—this test requires no knowledge of ground-truth features and can be run systematically across all atom pairs whose cosine similarity changed substantially during regularized retraining. A complementary diagnostic is per-input reconstruction loss decomposition: genuine near-duplicate features tend to appear on different input subsets (the model fires feature A on "Obama" tokens and feature B on "Barack Obama" multi-token spans), so repulsion-distorted atoms will show increased reconstruction error on inputs where the near-duplicate feature is active, detectable as a systematic loss spike concentrated on a semantically coherent input cluster rather than diffuse across the training distribution. The deeper problem is that the model's own feature geometry may violate the implicit assumption behind repulsion—Elhage et al.
